title: Death to the World and the New Creation
english: … put on incorruption. But if anyone is handed over to punishment, he is no better off than a naked man.

On 2 Corinthians 5:4: He means the thought to run on like this: we want to be clothed over with incorruption, not to strip off the body itself into corruption. That is why he added, “so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”
On 2 Corinthians 5:5: “For this very thing”: that is, for becoming incorruptible.
On 2 Corinthians 5:6: It stands for “being persuaded that while we are at home in the body,” that is, while we still live in the flesh in this world.

On 2 Corinthians 5:7: By faith we hope in God, for his form is not visible to us. But we believe that we will leave home and go to him, and then we will see him as far as a human being can see God. Moses, too, saw in a bodily way, and angels see as far as they are able to see; for no one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and every creature falls short of seeing God.

On 2 Corinthians 5:7–9: If you are pleasing here, beyond question you are more pleasing there, no longer struggling but secure in pleasing. It is also possible that “we walk by faith, not by sight” was said about the dispensation of God the Word, since Paul himself was not among those who had seen the Lord in the flesh before the passion.
On 2 Corinthians 5:12: Those who please people, and do not boast for the sake of reverence itself, plainly boast for show before people; for God watches the heart.

On 2 Corinthians 5:13: He calls boasting “being beside ourselves.” We boast so that he may be glorified; we say nothing of our boasting, and this he calls being of sound mind, so that we may teach you not to boast. He calls it “being beside oneself” when one who ought to shun boasting is forced to boast.
The second catena form adds: He means boasting about one's way of life. Boasting belongs to people who are beside themselves; moderation belongs to people of sound mind.

On 2 Corinthians 5:14–15: We would rather keep silent, but we are forced to boast, held fast by the love of Christ, so that he may be glorified. “All died”: he means the faithful, who are made dead to the world through baptism and through their way of life. “And no longer live for themselves”: for if I lived for myself, I would not boast either; but since I live for Christ, I keep silent for his sake when your good requires it, and for his sake I also boast, so that he may be glorified. “Whether we are beside ourselves,” he says, “or of sound mind for you,” we do everything because of the love of Christ. Now one who dies for others frees from death those already condemned, and as far as it lay with us, we were dead. If one died for all, then all died, as far as the sentence goes. He means the faithful, who through baptism were made dead to the world and no longer live for themselves but for Christ. For Christ, by dying for all and paying the common debt, made the world his debtor.

On 2 Corinthians 5:16: “So that from now on we know no one according to the flesh.” Circumcision belongs to the flesh, and so do “eat this” and “do not eat that,” and the sabbath; so he says that we who believe know no one according to the flesh. But since it could be objected that the Lord was circumcised and kept the sabbath, he says this at the right moment, to help those who are under the law. “But now we have not yet […] known this”: for he does not want us to live by the law. This was said not only to put our desires to death but also so that we no longer obey the law. For even if Christ was circumcised and came under the observances of the law, that is, “even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer.” When he was among men, he lived as a man and fulfilled the law in his life; but when he died and rose incorruptible, he abolished what belongs to the law and showed the way of the heavenly life. That is why the baptized, as people who have died, put to death the bodily ways of living, and by imitating the pure life of heaven they join themselves to God in their hearts.

On 2 Corinthians 5:17: If anyone lives in Christ and is baptized, he is a new creation, living no longer by the law but by the new grace of the Spirit. For whether you say law or grace, all things are from …

added_allusions.reason: Quotes “no one has ever seen God”.

title: Paul's exhortation and the Macedonian example
english: … God. For we do not say that the law is not from God, even if it has come to its end.
On 2 Corinthians 5:18: He says the preaching is a ministry of reconciliation; through it, when we believe, we will be reconciled to God.

On 2 Corinthians 5:19: It is to be understood like this: God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. So the punctuation should run: that God was, in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, that is, through Christ.

On 2 Corinthians 5:20: Now we are ambassadors in Christ's place, and God makes his appeal to you through us. Then he also shows that he is grieved over those who keep the law; for he says “on behalf of Christ,” not on behalf of the law. God appeals through us as through Christ, whose ministers and servants we are.

On 2 Corinthians 5:21: From here he showed how grieved he is over those who insist on keeping the law; for by keeping the law, he says, we have become sinners. Christ became sin to free us from sin. God has provided all this: receive the reconciliation, and give up keeping the ordinances of the law.
On 2 Corinthians 6:1: He entrusted the apostles not only with exhorting but also with working and toiling alongside them for salvation, so that they might receive God's grace sincerely.
On 2 Corinthians 6:4: He lays down endurance first, as an unbreakable foundation; once it is in place, any commandment can easily be built on it.

On 2 Corinthians 6:7: The weapons of righteousness on the right hand are holding fast to good works; those on the left are keeping away from evil works. Righteousness is achieved through both, for plainly, if one is missing, the other is left idle.
On 2 Corinthians 6:8: “Through glory” comes from those who receive the word and admire it, and “dishonor” from those who insult the believers. The same account holds for the phrases that follow.

On 2 Corinthians 6:11–13: When he says, “You are not restricted by us,” he means: we do not restrict you in the saving teaching, nor by holding anything back, for our heart has been opened wide and our mouth has opened to teach. So you too, in return, open your minds wide and take in the teaching; your heart has not opened wide enough to receive the teachings I give. So you are restricted by your own doing, unable to take in more precepts.

On 2 Corinthians 7:9: Receive us when we say, “so that you may suffer no loss from us in anything.” If I had kept silent, he says, and had not rebuked you, you would not have been grieved; and if you had not been grieved, you would have suffered loss by not repenting. I rejoice, he says, over your afflictions, because they are not worldly but spiritual. Next he recalls what happened to him in Asia for Christ's sake.

On 2 Corinthians 7:12: And yet he did write for this reason. But, as it seems, and as the outcome showed, “I was not writing for this reason, but so that your zeal and obedience might be shown.” So under the cover of one thing, another came to light.
On 2 Corinthians 7:13: He has been refreshed by this: they were obeying his teaching.

On 2 Corinthians 8:2: In the very thing in which they are sorely afflicted by persecution, he says, they rejoice the more, and their deep poverty overflowed into the wealth of their generosity. The apostle bears witness to the Macedonians that, poor as they were, they gave lavishly to good works, so that the Corinthians too might be stirred to bear fruit.

On 2 Corinthians 8:6: The Macedonians' eagerness for good works moved us to ask Titus to come to you, so that he might move you too to bear fruit. He also said “this” for this reason, since they had received the grace of teaching from him.
On 2 Corinthians 8:8: By “others” he means the Macedonians.

On 2 Corinthians 8:18–21: This should be joined to “we sent with him the brother whose praise is in the gospel,” so that they would be equal to administering the large and generous gift from the Gentiles, taking care and keeping watch, lest anyone blame us for standing in the way of the kindness meant for the saints. Before the Lord it is good to serve this kindness; before people it is good not to be blamed or slandered over so generous a ministry.

On 2 Corinthians 10:2–6: We do not preach to earn wages, the way the world's soldiers take their pay. “And being ready to punish all disobedience, when your obedience is complete”: since I knew that some are won over by word and exhortation, I did not want to use at once the severity I intend against some, because those who obey a word alone were not showing themselves. But first …

title: Defense of Apostolic Integrity and the Nature of Paul's Afflictions
english: … I rebuked with a word, so that those who correct themselves by it would be taught, and those who do not obey a word but need the severity of deeds would be exposed.

On 2 Corinthians 10:7: Test each one carefully by what the person's conduct is worth. This looks to the apostles. He was about to refute those of the circumcision, and they kept putting forward Peter, James and John; so he says, Be on your guard, so that the rank of these persons does not keep you from seeing the truth.

On 2 Corinthians 10:12: We write this without imitating those who commend themselves, for that is not good. They do not understand that they measure themselves by themselves and cannot stand comparison with anyone else; set beside others, they are nothing.
On 2 Corinthians 10:14: We are not cheap men boasting of great things beyond our own measure; for we did come as far as you and preached the word.

On 2 Corinthians 10:15–16: They boast of our labors; we do not. We boast, as is right, of the rule and the measure assigned to us, and we hope, as your faith grows, to preach the gospel even beyond you. By “rule” he means that he has come as far as them for the present.
On 2 Corinthians 10:17: Even if we boast, it is not as though we succeed by our own understanding, but by the grace of the Spirit.

On 2 Corinthians 11:2: You died to the law, he says, and you have become another man's, the one who rose from the dead (Romans 7:4). How then can she be a pure virgin, when she was married before? But born again through the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5), and passed into another life, she is rightly called a pure virgin.

On 2 Corinthians 11:4: Faith in Christ and the illumination of the Spirit confirm Christianity. So if you had not received these from [us], you would be right to look for those who still want to live by the law.

On 2 Corinthians 11:10–12: He says this not to reproach the Corinthians but to expose those who treat the preaching as a trade. That is why he says: I do not stop boasting that I have not made the preaching a trade, as they have; I have taken nothing from you and take nothing now. It is not that I do not love you, for I do; it is to cut away my accusers' pretext, so that, whether their boasting is false or true, they may be shown for what they are, as we have been shown.

On 2 Corinthians 12:2–5: This is strong proof that the soul is immortal; if he had known it to be mortal, he would not have doubted whether he saw the vision out of the body or in the body. By “as far as the third heaven” he meant the third part of the distance; for if he had gone up through three heavens, he would surely have heard the unspeakable words there and not in paradise. And let no one think that paradise lies above heaven: it was planted in the east, on earth, in the place called Eden, from where Adam too was formed, as Moses relates (Genesis 2:8). By “weaknesses” he means the persecutions, not a bodily illness, as some think.

On 2 Corinthians 12:7: Many suspect that he had a pain in his head, but in truth he means the persecutions, since the trials came from the devil's working. He called the trial that serves the devil “an angel of Satan,” by a metaphor from the angels who serve God. “Was given” must be understood as by God's permission, as in the case of Job; for God does not give evil things.
On 2 Corinthians 12:9: You have apostolic grace; do not ask to carry it out free of trials as well, for my power is made perfect in persecutions and afflictions.

On 2 Corinthians 12:13: Unless, then, you have this charge against me: that I took nothing from you for my keep and grew numb to my own want. If you think I sinned in this, pardon me, and forgive me the wrong you think I did you.
On 2 Corinthians 12:14: He calls them to witness this, concerning his coming to them a second and a third time because of the preaching.

On 2 Corinthians 13:4: Christ is said to have become sin and a curse (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13), though he was neither sin nor a curse; he made our evils his own in order to rescue us from them. In the same way he is now said to have been crucified through weakness: not his own, but the weakness he took on for us, as he managed everything for our sake.
